lines.text: In every village we had passed, the children shrieked when they saw Ash. Then they tried to ride him.
Here, a little girl looked up at a wolfhound the size of a horse, and looked away. As if nothing was worth the trouble.
Nobody worked the fields. Nobody talked. Grey faces sat in grey doorways, watching nothing.
Plague, my lord?
No cough. No fever. No new graves. Plague doesn't look like this.
At the end of the street stood the only new building in the village. Clean white stone. And over its door, seven rings around an eye.
The Order's mark. My lord, that's a tithe-house. I copied the orders for these at the College. I thought they were for grain.
They weren't. Through the open door, we watched the villagers go in one at a time, and hold a small white stone.
The stone glowed in each hand, soft as milk. And each of them came out a little greyer than they went in.
Tithe day, strangers. Every subject gives a little, so the kingdom stays warm. Move along.
As I rode past the fat little Measurer, his silver lens fogged white. He wiped it, and frowned, and watched me all the way down the street.
There's no tithe of aether in any law I ever studied.
Nor in the Charter. I'd know. So where does it all go?
I don't know. That frightens me more than the wyrm did.
That night we slept in a barn. A woman brought us soup, thin as rain. It was all they had. Her daughter held her skirt and never said a word.
My Tilda talked all day long, once. Then she turned seven, and they gave her the stone. She hasn't said a word since.
I wanted to claim the whole village. Ilse saw it on my face.
You can't, Lucan. Claim them and ride away, and you'll feel every one of them fading, all the way to Aldcrown.
Then just one. Will you trust me with her? I can't promise much. Only that she'll be warm.
If she can be warm, my lord, she's yours. We both are.
It was like pouring water into a bucket with no bottom. They'd been emptied so often. By midnight I was shaking, and the frost was back in my fingers.
In the morning, Tilda climbed onto Ash's back without asking. And laughed. Her mother sat down in the road and cried.
I sent them both north, with a note for Greyhollow. Ask for the steward with one arm, I told them. He'll pretend to be annoyed.
We rode on, a day late. Behind us, the little Measurer stood in the tithe-house door, and let a white bird go into the sky.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter sixty-three, coming soon.
